extracted.intended_audience: legal advocates, EPA rulemakers, federal courts, and public commenters on EPA rulemaking (notice-and-comment participants)
extracted.subtask_description: A legal comment arguing statutory-interpretation and evidentiary standards for EPA’s Section 202(a)(1) endangerment/contribute finding, explaining why EPA may not inject costs or policy considerations into the threshold inquiry and why contribution and endangerment are distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely scientific nature of Section 202(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a)(1)’s cause-or-contribute and endangerment questions are purely scientific in nature, and do not permit consideration of regulatory costs or other factors relevant (or irrelevant) to standard-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy factors (regulatory costs, climate adaptation opportunities, mitigation efforts, expected effectiveness of standards, or 'continued propriety' of EPA's regulatory program) cannot be imported into the Section 202(a)(1) inquiry. Courts (e.g., Coalition for Responsible Regulation; Massachusetts) treat the prism as a scientific judgment separate from later policy/implementation choices. EPA’s discussion must focus on whether emissions 'contribute' to and whether the pollutant 'endangers' public health/welfare, not on whether regulation would be wise or costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional language governs concurrency; absence of explicit 'simultaneous' language is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress intends findings and standards to be issued concurrently it uses clear, explicit language (e.g., NAAQS: Section 109(a)(2) requires EPA to 'publish, simultaneously with the issuance of such [air quality] criteria... proposed national primary and secondary ambient air quality standards'). Section 202 lacks such simultaneous/concurrent language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read words like 'simultaneous' into Section 202(a)(1). Analogies to other statutes that contain explicit simultaneity or expedited timing (e.g., Clean Water Act provisions requiring prompt proposals and finalization within 90 days) are inapt unless the statutory language is actually analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs belong in Section 202(a)(2), not in the Section 202(a)(1) threshold inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither Section 109(b) nor Section 202(a)(1)’s endangerment language references costs or implementation; both focus on public health and welfare. EPA must take costs into account when setting standards per Section 202(a)(2) (42 U.S.C. § 7521(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory cost considerations are properly presented and weighed during standard-setting (content, timing, stringency), not during the initial scientific determination whether the pollutant 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.' Prior EPA practice separates the 'Adverse Health and Welfare Effects' discussion from 'Economic Impact and Cost-effectiveness' sections in preambles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import broad 'appropriateness' precedents absent analogous statutory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Michigan v. EPA’s reading that 'appropriate' invites cost consideration concerned a different statutory phrase ('appropriate and necessary' under Section 112(n)(1)(A)) and does not apply to Section 202(a)(1), which lacks such broad language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency may not rely on cases interpreting different statutory terms as authority to incorporate cost-consideration into Section 202(a)(1) unless the statute contains comparable text; interpretive analogies must be textually grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the last-antecedent canon: the limiting clause modifies 'air pollution', not 'class or classes' or 'any air pollutant'
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatically, the restrictive clause ('which may be reasonably anticipated ...') in Section 202(a)(1) modifies 'air pollution,' not the immediately preceding nouns referencing vehicle classes or specific emitted pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule of the last antecedent and ordinary grammatical presumptions (Barnhart v. Thomas; Lopez v. Gonzales) when construing which phrase the limiting clause restricts. EPA's contrary reading that detaches the modifier from its natural antecedent is disfavored without extraordinary reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'contribute' — nontrivial / more-than-de-minimis standard; no unstated quantitative threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress included 'contribute' unmodified in Section 202(a)(1); 'contribute' by itself requires only a 'nontrivial' quantity of emissions (i.e., more than de minimis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not graft an additional statutory requirement that regulated emissions must 'cause or contribute to the danger... to a sufficient extent to satisfy the standard for regulation.' The statute contains no quantitative threshold for 'contribution' beyond the existing nontrivial/more-than-de-minimis standard (see Bluewater Network; Massachusetts). The 2009 Finding satisfied this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate and sequential treatment of the 'contribute' and 'endanger' prongs
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a)(1) contemplates two distinct inquiries: (1) whether particular 'air pollution' (e.g., greenhouse gases) may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare; and (2) whether motor-vehicle emissions 'cause, or contribute to' that endangerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat contribution (linking emissions to the identified dangerous pollution) and endangerment (danger posed by the pollutant class) as distinct, sequential scientific judgments. Case law (Coalition for Responsible Regulation; Ethyl Corp.; Massachusetts) supports this bifurcated approach and rejects collapsing them into a single policy-laden causal-chain test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate/class-based findings are permissible; statute permits combined determinations across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a)(1) refers to 'any class or classes of new motor vehicles or new motor vehicle engines,' indicating that EPA may make cause-or-contribute determinations based on the combined emissions of more than one vehicle category (up to all classes subject to regulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require separate threshold findings for each vehicle category absent statutory text. The plural 'classes' signals congressional intent to allow aggregate findings; legislative history explicitly contemplates consideration of all sources that 'contribute to air pollution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may not rewrite statute or insert omitted text to achieve preferred outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting Section 202(a)(1) in a way that requires moving, deleting, or adding entire clauses (e.g., inserting 'simultaneous' or a causation threshold) amounts to rewriting the statute—an authority only Congress possesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held agencies cannot reshape statutory text to reach preferred policy results (e.g., Nat. Res. Def. Council v. EPA; Louisiana Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. FCC; Lomax v. Ortiz-Marquez). Interpretations that necessitate deleting or relocating clauses or inserting new qualifying phrases are impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on drawing counterexamples from dissimilar statutory schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples like Clean Water Act provisions and NAAQS should not be treated as persuasive support for EPA’s reading of Section 202 when their language, structure, timing requirements, or purposes differ materially from Section 202.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare statutory text and context carefully: the CWA’s expedited timing ('prompt' proposal; 'within ninety days') reflects an express congressional purpose to expedite and differs from Section 202, which lacks similar urgency. Analogous structure and explicit wording are required before inferring that Congress intended a multi-step or concurrent process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific sufficiency for 'contribute' requires meaningful/measurable contribution; de minimis sources are excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: A source must meaningfully contribute to the dangerous pollutant mass to satisfy the 'contribute' prong; emissions that are truly de minimis (e.g., vehicle water vapor emissions) do not satisfy this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific evidence of atmospheric lifetimes, magnitudes, and mechanisms is required to show contribution. For example, vehicle water vapor emissions are scientifically de minimis (short atmospheric lifetime and negligible compared to natural evaporation) and therefore would not meet the contribution requirement even if elevated atmospheric water vapor were deemed dangerous. Use relevant scientific literature and quantitative estimates to demonstrate (non-)contribution.
